content:
Facts: Plaintiff sued siblings for dissolution of inheritance joint ownership claiming title derived from mother's inheritance and donation deed; failed to produce civil status documents, succession declaration, or family status certificate proving family relationship with deceased; defendant appeared contesting merits and counterclaiming for property keys.
Legal Framework: Articles 565, 732 Italian Civil Code (legitimate succession; intestate devolution); Art. 2697 (burden of proof); established case law on heir status proof requirements (Cass. 7276/2006, 14605/2005, 4414/1999, 12065/2014, 13738/2005, 19625/2003, SU 1114/2001).
Interpretive Issues: Whether family relationship constituting succession title must be proven via civil status documents regardless of defendant's non-contestation; relevance of succession declaration or substitute notoriety declaration for judicial heir status proof; whether intestate succession rules' non-negotiable nature requires ex officio verification of heir status despite parties' positions; allocation of burden to prove family relationship when exercising rights presupposing legitimate heir status.
Principles Applied: Legitimate succession title (family relationship per Art. 565) requires specific proof through civil status records demonstrating kinship with deceased. Succession declaration insufficient as purely fiscal document; substitute notoriety declaration potentially sufficient only per isolated case law when relationship undisputed. Family relationship proof mandatory via civil registry documents when disputed; some case law exempts proof when defendant raises no objection or raises it belatedly. Approach rejecting exemption merits support given intestate succession rules' non-negotiable nature and public relevance; Italian State holds supplementary heir position. Non-negotiable character renders parties' non-contestation completely irrelevant; judge must ascertain heir status ex officio regardless of adversarial positions. Procedural succession cases require heir status proof via civil documents irrespective of contestation; concerns proper adversarial process constitution and mandatory procedural public policy provisions. Ex officio verification essential for substantive merit assessment when plaintiff exercises right presupposing deceased's legitimate heir status; same mandatory non-negotiable nature applies to substantive intestate succession rules identifying State as last-resort successor. Approach requiring ex officio family relationship verification without regard to non-contestation prevents fraudulent collusion abuse through fictitious litigation prejudicing true legitimate heirs (third parties not proving alleged status). Division claim inadmissible absent timely proper civil status documentation production. Costs fully compensated given dispute nature and decision grounds.
